To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

grammars for indexed families can be learned behavior-ally correctly from computably noisy positive data, and grammars for indexed classes can be learned behaviorially correctly from computably, noisily, positively and negatively data, where the noise-tolerant learners are synthesized by the indices for the classes.

computable noise-tolerance is a very strong property of learners and that, in particular, it is not possible to synthesize a computable noise-tolernat learner from an index for a family of recursive languages that is not computable noise-tolorant.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the computability-theoretic aspects of the synthesis of language-learners tolerant of computable noisy input data sequences.
the synthesis of language learners tolerating computable noisy data.
the following questions: what kinds of learners can be synthesized from indices for r. e. classes and for recursive indexed families of languages? and how do these synthesizers work?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
computable noisy data, though not as clean as computable noiseless data, is still clean enough to permit synthesis of language-learners.

the synthesis of noise-tolerants, from indices for classes and families indexed, for the computably noisy data case, can be accomplished in many interesting cases, and in some interesting cases, it cannot.

the synthesis of noise-tolerating behaviorally correct language-learners from indices for r. e. classes of languages, or for indexed families of languages, is a very difficult problem, and that, in fact, the only positive synthesis results obtained are for grammars and for indexed families, and even for grammars, only for computable noisy data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, under our restriction, the computable, noisy data restriction does not affect the computable noise-free data learnability of the corresponding families.
the computable noise tolerance assumption, which is a reasonable assumption, does not make the learning of grammars from noisy data any more difficult than learning grammars from noiseless data.

, for the synthesis of noise-tolerating learners for indexed families, we are in a position to say that, if the family indexed has the telltale property for the computable, noisy positive and negative input data, then such learners can be synthesized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a computable world, the synthesis of learners tolerating noisy data is possible.
, for the computability restriction on noisy data, there are positive synthesis results that do not exist for the general noisy data case.

computability restrictions on noisy data sequences, in addition to the computability restrictions on the synthesizers themselves, are necessary to achieve positive results regarding the computable noise tolerance of language learners.
